title: AI job disruption priced into man's compensation payout in first known case
full_text:
Artificial intelligence's disruptive impact on jobs was priced into an almost $1 million injury claim after a car accident left a NSW man with reduced working capacity.
It's the first known case of a legal body explicitly considering the impact of AI on the workforce when calculating a worker's future earnings.
Earlier this month, the NSW Personal Injury Commission assessed that Andrew Duong suffered damages of $950,000 after he suffered both physical and psychological injuries following a head-on collision on his way to work in 2023.
This included the 34-year-old's $400,000 of future economic loss after finding he could only continue working with restrictions, and the injuries and pain would impact his ability to find future employment if he could no longer work at his current job.
Commission member Philip Carr wrote that Mr Duong had 33 years of working life ahead of him that would be affected by his loss of capacity.
Mr Carr determined that Mr Duong should receive a "significant buffer" for the uncertainty around future loss of earnings, which included the impact of AI.
"[And] with the uncertainty of any occupation in today's workforce, especially with the advent of artificial intelligence and its workplace challenges during his working life, which requires an allowance for his future continuing loss of capacity," he wrote.
The tribunal did not find that AI had cost Mr Duong work, or predict that it would, only that AI may create more job market uncertainty that could disproportionately affect an injured worker with need for greater accommodations.
Before the crash, Mr Duong was working about 70 hours a week in warehouse roles for Aldi and Home Delivery Service.
The crash caused injuries to his right hand and wrist, shoulder, elbow and lower back, as well as a psychological injury. He had two operations on his wrist.
Mr Duong lost his Aldi job after the crash because he was not cleared to return to full-time work, but was still employed by the delivery company on reduced hours.
Mr Carr found Mr Duong could continue in that role with restrictions but said his prospects on the open labour market would be "considerably reduced" if he lost it.
Artificial intelligence was one of multiple considerations mentioned by Mr Carr when assessing Duong's capacity to earn, alongside his injuries, medication and the risk of losing his current role.
How will AI impact future jobs?
Queensland University of Technology's associate professor in economics, Dr Leonora Risse, said there was a lot of uncertainty about how AI would influence the job market.
"There's no one definitive clear result. In some ways it'll be positive, in other aspects, it will be negative," she said.
Dr Rissa said even if certain jobs or industries were not threatened by automation, there would still likely be an impact on the tasks that comprise a job and the skills required.
"Work and tasks are going to look very different," she said, adding that the job market has always been in flux as a result of technological change.
The decision comes after the federal government recently released its first ever analysis of AI's impact on the jobs market, which found no evidence of broad AI-driven disruption in Australia's labour market so far.
Modelling by the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations suggested employment in a more AI-exposed occupation was about 2 per cent lower by February than under its pre-ChatGPT trend.
But the department repeatedly cautioned that this was not proof AI had caused job losses. Jobs exposed to the technology had already been growing more slowly before ChatGPT became widely available.
The government said it would continue monitoring the data as more evidence became available.
